extracted.intended_audience: readers, editors, and scholars of 18th-century periodical essays (Samuel Johnson/Adventurer & Idler)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and critical guidance for composing and judging 18th‑century periodical essays (the Adventurer and the Idler), focusing on style, moral purpose, topicality, tone, and authorship/attribution. The page is a prefatory critical notice that articulates what makes these essays effective or faulted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rambler style and sentiments as model
rubrics_metrics.description: “The style and sentiments of the Rambler, which evidently, from his commencement, he made the models of his imitation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Johnson's Adventurer papers are to be read as a continuation of the Rambler: expect similar moral tone, diction, and argumentative manner. When producing or evaluating such essays, judge fidelity to high moral and philosophical style and the successful adaptation of the Rambler's tone to new contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thematic focus on literature, literary men, and moral critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjects discussed include 'the interests of literature and of literary men, the emptiness of praise and the vanity of human wishes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essays should engage with questions about literature and literary culture, expose the emptiness of superficial praise, and interrogate human ambition. Evaluate pieces on how persuasively and insightfully they treat these topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intimate knowledge of town manners
rubrics_metrics.description: The papers 'display intimate knowledge, of the town and its manners.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective periodical essays incorporate accurate, observant depictions of contemporary urban life and manners; assess the vividness, accuracy, and usefulness of such social observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of humorous delineation of adventure and character
rubrics_metrics.description: The essays are 'occasionally we are amused with humorous delineation of adventure and of character.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ vivid, often comic character sketches or episodic adventures to illuminate moral or social points. Example: No.84's stage-coach journey is cited as exemplary. Judge humor by its capacity to instruct or reveal, not merely to entertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety of subjects to broaden appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: From the greater variety of its subjects... the sale of the Adventurer was greater than that of the Rambler on its first appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A wider range of topics can increase readership and contemporary appeal. When assessing essays aimed at periodical audiences, consider whether subject variety is balanced with coherence and moral purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of party-politics and personal censure
rubrics_metrics.description: Works that 'deal not in party-politics, nor exemplify their ethical discussions by holding out living characters to censure or contempt' are favoured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer general moral argumentation to partisan polemic or direct attacks on living individuals. Anti-pattern: using essays primarily to vilify named contemporaries or to pursue party aims at the expense of broader moral reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benevolent moral purpose — admonish and benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: Johnson embraced 'any opportunity of promoting the interests of morality and virtue' and wrote 'to admonish and to benefit'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Periodical essays should aim to improve readers morally or intellectually. Evaluate whether the piece's purpose is reformative and benevolent rather than merely provocative or sensational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity in moral stance; no facile compromise
rubrics_metrics.description: Here is 'no compromise of personal sensuality, for an endurance of others' frailties, amounting to an indifference of moral distinctions altogether.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral pronouncements should be sincere and principled; avoid equivocating moral standards in order to excuse vice. Assess the essay's ethical consistency and seriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground moral arguments in religious/moral duty rather than worldly incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Johnson 'ever directs our attention... to the discharge of the duty which Providence assigns us' rather than to 'the world's smile or frown.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When treating conduct and virtue, favour arguments grounded in duty or higher principle, not merely in reputation or worldly reward. Evaluate the depth and seriousness of the ethical grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate stylistic scale for subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘In his sublime discussions of the most sacred truths, as no style can be too lofty nor conceptions too grand for such a subject...’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match diction, tone, and rhetorical ambition to the gravity of the subject: sacred or deeply serious topics warrant elevated style, while lighter subjects allow a plainer register. Judge alignment of style and subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt tone to occasion — philosophic reproof or cheerful social voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Johnson 'accommodated himself to the circumstances in which he was placed, and diligently sought to avail himself of each varying opportunity to admonish and to benefit, whether from the chair of philosophic reproof or in the cheerful, social circle.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective writers vary tone according to audience and context, from solemn admonition to playful irony, while maintaining moral purpose. Evaluate flexibility and appropriateness of tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of lax conversational tone that leads to misconstruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Johnson himself admitted 'Nobody at times... talks more laxly than I do.' Such laxity 'may well be presumed to have affected the humorous and almost conversational tone of the work' and led to misconstruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conversational ease is useful but can produce careless statements later misinterpreted; assess whether casual phrasing undermines clarity or invites unjust controversy. Anti-pattern: glib paradoxes or 'sophistry' offered as sport that later require retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire should reform, not merely wound
rubrics_metrics.description: He 'never wounds feeling for the sake of raising a laugh, nor sports with folly, but in the hope of reclaiming the vicious and with the design of warning the young.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satirical elements must aim at correction or warning rather than gratuitous cruelty. Evaluate whether ridicule is ethically justified and pedagogically useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affectation of sentimentality; prefer dignified sorrow
rubrics_metrics.description: On mourning: 'Here is no affectation of sentimentality, no morbid and puling complaints, but the dignified and chastened expression of sorrow.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotive writing should be restrained and authentic rather than mawkish. Judge pathos by its restraint and truthfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vivid episodic description to exemplify points
rubrics_metrics.description: The Preface cites No.84's 'description... of the incidents of a stage-coach journey' as exemplary and often imitated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete narrative episodes and descriptive scene-making can powerfully illustrate abstract moral points; evaluate clarity, vividness, and illustrative force of such episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear documentation/attribution when multiple contributors involved
rubrics_metrics.description: On authorship: 'in Dr. Warton's copy... the following remark was found at the end: "The papers marked T were written by Mr. S. Johnson."' Boswell's internal evidence was unnecessary because of this attribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When periodicals have multiple contributors, mark and document authorship to aid attribution. For editors: preserve or provide clear attributions and notes on provenance; for critics: prefer documentary evidence to speculative internal attribution.
